entities.summary:
The Boxer Rebellion was a pivotal anti-imperialist uprising that took place in China from 1899 to 1901, led by the Righteous and Harmonious Fists, also known as the Boxers. The rebellion was sparked by a combination of factors, including economic hardship, foreign influence, and a desire for Chinese nationalism and traditional values.

The Boxers, who were largely peasants and artisans, sought to expel foreign influence, including Christian missionaries and Chinese converts to Christianity, from China. They also targeted Chinese who had learned Western skills, such as modern medicine and mechanics.

The Boxers were eventually defeated by an international coalition of troops, including those from the United States, Japan, and Europe, in the Battle of Peking on August 14, 1900. The Boxer Protocol, signed in 1901, imposed harsh penalties on China and further weakened the Qing dynasty.

The Boxer Rebellion marked the end of the imperial era in China and paved the way for the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1912, which ultimately led to the establishment of the Republic of China. The rebellion also highlighted the tensions between China and the Western world, which would continue to shape the country's relations with the West for decades to come.

In the end, the Boxer Rebellion was a tragic and bloody attempt to resist the forces of modernity and imperialism, but it ultimately failed to achieve its goals and left China weakened and vulnerable to further foreign intervention.
